question: According to the Connecticut CDL manual, how far can the school bus danger zone extend from the front bumper of the bus?
choice_a: As much as 50 feet, with the last 10 feet being the most dangerous
choice_b: Only the width of the bus itself
choice_c: As much as 30 feet, with the first 10 feet being the most dangerous
choice_d: Exactly 10 feet, with no distinction in danger level
explanation: The manual states the danger zone may extend as much as 30 feet from the front bumper, with the first 10 feet being the most dangerous, in addition to 10 feet along each side and 10 feet behind the rear bumper.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-1

question: Which side of a school bus is always considered part of the danger zone, regardless of distance, because of passing traffic?
choice_a: The left side of the bus
choice_b: The right side of the bus
choice_c: The roof of the bus
choice_d: Only the rear of the bus
explanation: The manual specifically notes that the area to the left of the bus is always considered dangerous because of passing cars.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-1

question: Per the manual, the blind spot directly behind a school bus typically extends about how far, and could extend even farther depending on the bus's length and width?
choice_a: 5 to 10 feet, possibly up to 20 feet
choice_b: 50 to 150 feet, possibly up to 400 feet
choice_c: 500 to 600 feet, possibly up to 1,000 feet
choice_d: There is no blind spot behind a school bus
explanation: The manual explains there is a blind spot immediately below and in front of each side mirror and directly behind the rear bumper, and that the blind spot behind the bus extends 50 to 150 feet and could extend up to 400 feet depending on the length and width of the bus.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-1

topic: Use of Mirrors - Flat Mirror Adjustment
question: When properly adjusted, the outside left and right side flat mirrors should allow the driver to see how far behind the school bus?
choice_a: 100 feet or 2 bus lengths
choice_b: 500 feet or 10 bus lengths
choice_c: 50 feet or 1 bus length
choice_d: 200 feet or 4 bus lengths
explanation: The manual states that properly adjusted outside flat mirrors should let the driver see 200 feet or 4 bus lengths behind the bus, along the sides of the bus, and the rear tires touching the ground.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-1

question: What is a key characteristic of the outside left and right side convex mirrors on a school bus, according to the manual?
choice_a: They provide an exact, true-to-size reflection of objects near the bus
choice_b: They are mounted on the rear bumper of the bus
choice_c: They present a view of people and objects that does not accurately reflect their size and distance from the bus
choice_d: They are used only to monitor the interior of the bus
explanation: The manual notes that the convex mirrors, mounted below the outside flat mirrors, monitor the sides at a wide angle but present a view of people and objects that does not accurately reflect their true size and distance from the bus.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-2

question: The outside left and right side crossover mirrors on a school bus are primarily used to see what area?
choice_a: The front bumper "danger zone" directly in front of the bus that is not visible by direct vision
choice_b: The interior aisle and seats of the bus
choice_c: The area directly above the roof of the bus
choice_d: The rear emergency exit door only
explanation: The manual explains the crossover mirrors are mounted at the front corners of the bus and are used to see the front bumper danger zone not visible by direct vision, as well as the danger zone to the left and right sides, including the service door and front wheel area.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-2

topic: Use of Mirrors - Overhead Rearview Mirror
question: The overhead inside rearview mirror, mounted above the windshield on a school bus, is used mainly for what purpose?
choice_a: Monitoring passenger activity inside the bus
choice_b: Monitoring traffic in the oncoming lane only
choice_c: Viewing the front bumper danger zone
choice_d: Checking the rear tires for proper inflation
explanation: The manual states the overhead inside rearview mirror is used to monitor passenger activity inside the bus, and that the driver should be able to see the top of the rear window and all of the students, including those seated right behind the driver.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-3

question: If the school bus is so equipped, when should the driver activate the alternating flashing amber warning lights when approaching a stop?
choice_a: Immediately after the stop signal arm is extended
choice_b: Only after the bus has come to a complete stop
choice_c: At least 500 feet before the stop, regardless of speed
choice_d: At least 200 feet or approximately 5-10 seconds before the school bus stop, or in accordance with state law
explanation: The manual instructs that alternating flashing amber warning lights should be activated at least 200 feet, or approximately 5-10 seconds, before the school bus stop, or in accordance with state law.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-3

question: When stopping to load students, how far away from the students at the designated stop should the school bus's front bumper be positioned?
choice_a: At least 10 feet, forcing students to walk to the bus
choice_b: Right at the curb, touching the students' position
choice_c: There is no specified distance
choice_d: At least 25 feet, so students have time to gather
explanation: The manual states the driver should bring the bus to a full stop with the front bumper at least 10 feet away from students at the designated stop, which forces students to walk to the bus so the driver has a better view of their movements.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-3

question: During loading procedures, what should the driver do regarding the students waiting at the bus stop?
choice_a: Allow students to board without counting them, to save time
choice_b: Only count students who are riding for the first time
choice_c: Count the number of students at the bus stop and be sure all board the bus
choice_d: Count students only after the bus has left the stop
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to count the number of students at the bus stop and be sure all board the bus, and if possible to know the names of students at each stop so a missing student can be identified.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-4

question: During unloading procedures on the route, how far should students be told to walk from the side of the bus after exiting?
choice_a: The manual does not specify a distance
choice_b: At least 50 feet, before looking back at the bus
choice_c: At least 10 feet, to a position where the driver can plainly see them
choice_d: 2 feet, staying as close to the bus as possible
explanation: The manual states that students should be told to exit the bus and walk at least 10 feet away from the side of the bus to a position where the driver can plainly see all students.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-4

question: When a student must cross the roadway in front of the school bus, where should the student walk to before crossing?
choice_a: At least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper, while staying away from the front of the bus
choice_b: Directly in front of the driver's side window
choice_c: To the rear bumper of the bus and around the back
choice_d: Onto the roadway immediately upon exiting the bus
explanation: The manual directs students to walk to a location at least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper, while still remaining away from the front of the school bus, and to wait for the driver's signal before crossing.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-4

topic: Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading
question: If a student drops an object near the bus during loading or unloading, what should the student be told to do?
choice_a: Ask another student to retrieve the object for them
choice_b: Immediately pick up the object before continuing
choice_c: Wait at the danger zone until the driver notices the object
choice_d: Leave the object and move to a point of safety out of the danger zones, then try to get the driver's attention
explanation: The manual warns that stopping to pick up a dropped object may cause a student to disappear from the driver's sight at a dangerous moment, so students should be told to leave the object and move to safety, then attempt to get the driver's attention to retrieve it.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-5

topic: Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading
question: What safety hazard does the manual describe under "Handrail Hang-ups"?
choice_a: Handrails being too short for taller students to reach
choice_b: Students slipping because handrails are not present on school buses
choice_c: Students being injured or killed when clothing, accessories, or body parts get caught in the handrail or door as they exit the bus
choice_d: Handrails becoming loose and detaching from the bus
explanation: The manual states students have been injured or killed when clothing, accessories, or parts of their body got caught in the handrail or door while exiting, so drivers should closely observe exiting students to confirm they are in a safe location before moving the bus.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-5

question: Under which of the following conditions must a school bus driver evacuate the bus, according to the manual?
choice_a: Two students have a minor verbal disagreement
choice_b: The bus is stalled on or adjacent to a railroad-highway crossing
choice_c: The bus is running 10 minutes behind schedule
choice_d: It has started to lightly rain
explanation: The manual lists mandatory evacuation conditions including the bus being on fire or threatened by fire, being stalled on or adjacent to a railroad-highway crossing, imminent danger of collision, the bus's position changing to increase danger, or a need to evacuate due to a hazardous materials spill.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-6

question: According to the manual, a "safe place" for evacuated students should be located how far from the road?
choice_a: At least 100 feet off the road, in the direction of oncoming traffic
choice_b: At least 10 feet off the road, on either side
choice_c: Directly beside the evacuated bus
choice_d: At least 500 feet off the road, away from the bus route
explanation: The manual states a safe place will be at least 100 feet off the road in the direction of oncoming traffic, which keeps students from being hit by debris if another vehicle collides with the bus.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-6

question: If there is a risk from a hazardous materials spill during an evacuation, how far upwind of the bus should students be led?
choice_a: At least 300 feet
choice_b: At least 50 feet
choice_c: At least 100 feet
choice_d: At least 1,000 feet
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to lead students upwind of the bus at least 300 feet if there is a risk from spilled hazardous materials.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-6

question: As part of securing the bus before ordering an evacuation, which of the following should the driver do?
choice_a: Leave the transmission in Drive in case the bus needs to be moved quickly
choice_b: Leave the engine running so the hazard lights stay powered
choice_c: Leave the ignition key in place for the next driver
choice_d: Place the transmission in Park (or Neutral if there is no Park position), set the parking brakes, shut off the engine, remove the ignition key, and activate hazard-warning lights
explanation: The manual's general evacuation procedures instruct the driver to secure the bus by placing the transmission in Park or Neutral, setting the parking brakes, shutting off the engine, removing the ignition key, and activating hazard-warning lights.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-7

question: What distinguishes a "passive" railroad-highway crossing from an "active" crossing, according to the manual?
choice_a: There is no meaningful difference between the two
choice_b: A passive crossing has no traffic control device, so the decision to proceed rests entirely with the driver
choice_c: A passive crossing always has flashing lights and gates
choice_d: An active crossing has no warning signs of any kind
explanation: The manual explains that a passive crossing does not have any type of traffic control device, requiring the driver to recognize the crossing, search for a train, and decide if it is safe to cross, whereas an active crossing has installed devices such as flashing lights, bells, and gates.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-7

question: What does encountering a cross-buck sign at a railroad crossing require a school bus driver to do?
choice_a: Only slow down; a full stop is never required at a cross-buck sign
choice_b: Proceed without stopping as long as no train is currently visible
choice_c: Yield the right-of-way to the train, and stop before the sign if there is no painted white stop line
choice_d: Sound the horn continuously while crossing the tracks
explanation: The manual states the cross-buck sign marks the crossing and requires the driver to yield the right-of-way to the train, and if there is no white line painted on the pavement, the driver must stop the bus before the cross-buck sign.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-8

question: If the gate at a railroad crossing stays down after the train has passed, what does the manual say the driver should do?
choice_a: Honk the horn repeatedly until the gate lifts on its own
choice_b: Back the bus up and find an alternate route immediately
choice_c: Carefully drive around the gate once the train is gone
choice_d: Not drive around the gate, and instead call the dispatcher
explanation: The manual instructs that if the gate stays down after the train passes, the driver should not drive around the gate but should instead call the dispatcher.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-8

question: At a railroad-highway crossing, where should the school bus stop in relation to the nearest rail?
choice_a: At least 100 feet from the nearest rail
choice_b: Exactly 5 feet from the nearest rail
choice_c: No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail
choice_d: As close as possible to the cross-buck sign, touching the rail if necessary
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail, at the point offering the best view of the tracks.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-9

topic: Railroad Crossing - Bus Stalled on Tracks
question: If a school bus stalls or becomes trapped on railroad tracks, what does the manual instruct the driver to do?
choice_a: Get everyone off the bus and off the tracks immediately, moving away at an angle that is both away from the tracks and toward the direction of the oncoming train
choice_b: Keep all students on the bus and wait for roadside assistance
choice_c: Attempt to push the bus off the tracks before evacuating anyone
choice_d: Move everyone away from the tracks but in the same direction the train is coming from behind them
explanation: The manual states that if the bus stalls or is trapped on the tracks, the driver should get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving everyone away from the bus at an angle that is both away from the tracks and toward the train.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-9

question: According to the manual's guidance on handling serious student behavior problems, where may a driver put a student off the bus?
choice_a: Only at the nearest police station
choice_b: Only at school or at the student's designated school bus stop
choice_c: At any location along the route the driver considers appropriate
choice_d: At the nearest gas station or rest area
explanation: The manual states a driver should never put a student off the bus except at school or at his or her designated school bus stop, and if the offense is serious enough, should call for a school administrator or the police instead.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-9

question: Per the DOT requirement referenced in the manual, air-braked school buses (as well as trucks and trailers) must be equipped with antilock braking systems (ABS) if built on or after what date?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: March 1, 1999
choice_c: January 1, 2000
choice_d: July 1, 2017
explanation: The manual states the Department of Transportation requires ABS on air brake vehicles, including trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies, built on or after March 1, 1998 (with hydraulically braked trucks and buses of 10,000 lbs GVWR or more required as of March 1, 1999).
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-10

question: When a school bus driver posts a lookout to assist with backing the bus, what is the lookout's role according to the manual?
choice_a: To physically guide the bus with hand signals directing every turn
choice_b: To operate the bus's hazard warning lights during the backing maneuver
choice_c: To warn the driver about obstacles, approaching persons, and other vehicles, but not to give directions on how to back the bus
choice_d: To count students boarding the bus while it backs up
explanation: The manual explains that the purpose of a lookout when backing is to warn the driver about obstacles, approaching persons, and other vehicles, and that the lookout should not give directions on how to back the bus. Backing is strongly discouraged and should only be done when there is no other safe way to move the bus.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 10 - School Bus, p. 10-11
